title: Music for the Royal Fireworks
hook: A king who wanted “no fiddles”, a band of more than fifty wind players and drummers, and music written to open a fireworks night in London.

painting.title: The Annual Girandola at the Castel Sant’Angelo, Rome
painting.pairingNote: A great public fireworks display of the 18th century, rockets bursting over a castle at night in clouds of smoke, the kind of spectacle Handel’s music was written to open.

facts: In 1748 the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle ended the War of the Austrian Succession, and King George II ordered a huge fireworks display in London’s Green Park to celebrate. Handel, settled in London for nearly forty years, was asked for the music. It opened the celebration on 27 April 1749.

The king wanted only “martial” instruments, wind and drums, and hoped there would be “no fiddles”. Handel, who wanted strings, gave way. He wrote for 24 oboes, 12 bassoons and a contrabassoon, 9 trumpets, 9 horns, timpani and side drums, about sixty players.

Six days earlier a public rehearsal in Vauxhall Gardens drew a crowd said to number twelve thousand, and carriages were stuck for three hours on London Bridge. The fireworks night itself went badly: it rained, many rockets misfired, and one of the wooden pavilions caught fire. The music was the success of the evening.

A month later Handel performed the suite at the Foundling Hospital, a London home for abandoned children, and added strings. Most performances today use that later version. This recording goes back to the original band, without strings.

It is a French-style [[suite|suite]]: a grand overture followed by dances. In one line: a grand ceremonial overture (I), a brisk dance (II), a gentle picture of peace (III), a shout of joy (IV), two minuets, one soft and one festive (V).

movements.heading: Ouverture
movements.title: Ouverture
movements.summary: By far the longest movement, more than a third of the suite. It is a [[french-overture|French overture]]: a slow, majestic opening in jerky, dotted rhythms, with trumpets and drums, then a fast section of fanfares. A short, slower passage in a minor key interrupts it, and the fast music returns to finish.

mainIdeas.name: The ceremony
mainIdeas.description: slow, grand chords in long-short rhythms, the whole band with trumpets and drums.

mainIdeas.name: The echoes
mainIdeas.description: phrases answered softly by smaller groups, as if from a distance.

mainIdeas.name: The fanfares
mainIdeas.description: a fast, bright section built on trumpet calls.

stops.hear: Slow, grand chords in a jerky long-short rhythm; trumpets and drums ring out over a mass of oboes and bassoons
stops.happening: The ceremonial opening of the [[french-overture|French overture]]

stops.hear: Phrases thrown back and forth, loud then soft, like echoes
stops.happening: Groups of the band answering each other

stops.hear: The tempo jumps: quick, bright trumpet calls, answered by the oboes, and the drums driving
The music turns briefly towards a minor key, still fast
stops.happening: The middle part of the Allegro

stops.hear: Suddenly slower and quieter, in a darker key; the trumpets and drums fall silent
stops.happening: The Lentement, for oboes and bassoons

stops.hear: The fast fanfares return
stops.happening: The Allegro again, to the end

notice: Listen to how many oboes play together. With a dozen on the top line, the sound is thick and reedy, nothing like a modern orchestra.

movements.heading: Bourrée
movements.title: Bourrée
movements.summary: A short, quick dance in D minor, in two beats, without the trumpets and drums: a moment of lighter music after the ceremony.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a brisk tune with a skipping upbeat, played by oboes over the bassoons.

stops.hear: A quick, lightly skipping tune in a minor key, oboes over bassoons
A longer second phrase that wanders and comes home
stops.happening: The second half of the dance

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The dance once more, from the beginning
stops.happening: The return of the first part

notice: Notice the silence of the brass. After the overture, the band without trumpets and drums sounds almost like a different ensemble.

movements.heading: La Paix
movements.title: La Paix
movements.summary: “Peace”: a slow, rocking movement in the lilting rhythm of a [[siciliano|siciliano]], the calm centre of the suite. Horns join the oboes and bassoons, and the music gives a gentle, almost pastoral picture of the peace the fireworks celebrated.

mainIdeas.name: The rocking tune
mainIdeas.description: a slow melody in a swaying long-short rhythm, in the oboes.

mainIdeas.name: The horns
mainIdeas.description: warm, held notes underneath and between the phrases.

stops.hear: A slow, swaying tune in the oboes; soft horns hold notes beneath
The same first half again
A new phrase that rises a little and turns back

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The tune settles; the horns hold the last chord

notice: Listen for the horns. They hardly have a tune of their own, but their round, soft sound gives the movement its warmth.

movements.heading: La Réjouissance
movements.title: La Réjouissance
movements.summary: “Rejoicing”: a short, brilliant movement in D major with all the trumpets and drums. It begins with the trumpets entering one after another on the same call, each a little higher, and the whole tune is played through more than once, each time by a different combination of the band.

mainIdeas.name: The trumpet call
mainIdeas.description: a short rising figure that the three trumpet parts start one after another.

mainIdeas.name: The full band
mainIdeas.description: oboes, horns, bassoons and drums joining for a festive tutti.

stops.hear: Trumpets enter one after another with the same bright call, drums beneath
A longer second phrase, still loud and festive
The tune starts again; listen for which instruments carry it this time
stops.happening: The second time through, in a new colour

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The whole band with drums, as loud as it gets

notice: In the first seconds, count the trumpet entries: the same call comes three times, each one starting before the last has finished.

movements.heading: Menuets I and II
movements.title: Menuets I and II
movements.summary: The suite ends with two minuets. The first, in D minor, is soft and graceful, for oboes and bassoons. The second, in D major, brings back the trumpets, horns and drums and ends the suite in a festive mood.

mainIdeas.name: Menuet I
mainIdeas.description: a graceful dance in three, in a minor key, without the brass.

mainIdeas.name: Menuet II
mainIdeas.description: the same kind of dance in a major key, bright and ceremonial.

stops.hear: A gentle dance in three, in a minor key, oboes over bassoons
The key brightens to major; horns and trumpets take over

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The second minuet closes, loud and bright

notice: Compare the two minuets. They have the same rhythm and nearly the same length; only the key and the instruments change, and the mood changes completely.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Trevor Pinnock gathered a band the size of Handel’s own in 1749: more than fifty wind players and drummers, with no strings, recorded in Watford in 1996.

threads.title: Wind and drums
threads.body: Without strings, the music is all reeds, brass and percussion, the sound of a military band built for the open air.

threads.title: Loud and soft
threads.body: The suite alternates movements with trumpets and drums (I, IV, the second minuet) and gentler ones without them (II, III, the first minuet).

threads.title: A celebration of peace
threads.body: Two movements have titles: “La Paix” (“Peace”) and “La Réjouissance” (“Rejoicing”). They name the occasion the fireworks celebrated.
